title: Maximus the Confessor
hookLine: punished, tradition says, for teaching that Christ had a human will; he saw the whole cosmos as a liturgy

lines: THE MOUNT OF OLIVES, AT NIGHT.
cards: Night, on the Mount of Olives. Jesus walks about a stone's throw from his friends and kneels down to pray.
Luke gives the words: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Not my will. So he had one.
A monk named Maximus read that line and wouldn't let it go, and tradition says it cost him dearly. He's remembered as the Confessor.

teach.b: In Maximus's day, a teaching was spreading that Christ had only one will. It was meant to keep the peace between quarreling churches. Maximus said no.

If the Son of God became fully human, he became human all the way down, and a human being has a human will. In the garden we hear that will speak: remove this cup. Then we hear it freely say yes: not my will, but thine.
That yes, Maximus taught, is where a human will is healed, not erased. Tradition says he was put on trial, refused to back down, and was punished with terrible cruelty and sent into exile.
So he's called Confessor: someone who suffered for confessing the faith. And he saw a larger picture.
Every created thing, he taught, has its own word, its own reason for being, from the one Word who made it: a stone, a sparrow, a person. All of it is meant to be gathered back to God.
Ephesians speaks of God gathering "together in one all things in Christ."
Maximus saw the church at worship as a small model of that whole, and the whole world as a kind of worship. Some readers sum up his vision as a cosmic liturgy.

That closes a week of great thinkers: Athanasius on why the Word became flesh, the Cappadocians' three and one, Augustine's restless heart and his picture of love, Boethius and the wheel, Dionysius and the ladder of names.
And now Maximus: a human will saying yes, inside a universe at prayer.

how: Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor Maximus as a saint; Christians of different churches pray Jesus's words from Gethsemane, "not my will, but thine," when facing a hard choice.

o: a monk who heard confessions for a whole city
an emperor who settled a quarrel between churches
a monk who held that Christ had a human will

p: has its own word from the Word

s: Maximus taught that Christ had only a divine will
he taught the opposite: Christ, fully human, had a human will, which freely said yes in the garden.
in the garden, Jesus asks for the cup to be taken away
"remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done."
it's a title for someone who suffered for confessing the faith.

games.q: you're Maximus. a teaching that Christ had only one will is meant to keep the peace between churches. what do you do?
o: go along with it for the sake of peace.
say no: a fully human Christ had a human will.
games.why: Maximus refused. tradition says he was tried, punished with cruelty, and exiled for it, which is why the church calls him Confessor.

practice: Notice one thing you want badly right now, big or small, and name it plainly; Jesus didn't pretend in the garden. If you pray, you can say his words from Luke: not my will, but thine, be done.
If you don't, hold the wanting with an open hand instead of a fist, and breathe around it.

wordCard.voice: Maximus the Confessor. A monk who taught that Christ had a real human will that freely said yes, and who saw all creation gathered into worship.

orig.note: Greek: word, reason. Maximus taught that each created thing has its own logos from the one Logos, the Word.

carryVoice: Your line: a cosmic liturgy. In Maximus's eyes, even a sparrow belongs to the worship. Go gently.
